title: AWS Lambda
description: Learn the fundamentals of AWS Lambda including runtimes, handlers, layers, environment variables, IAM roles, concurrency, and versions.

data.text: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs your code in response to events. You upload your code as a function, and Lambda automatically provisions and scales the underlying infrastructure. You only pay for the compute time you consume.
A Lambda function is code packaged with configuration. Lambda supports multiple runtimes including Python, Node.js, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET, and custom runtimes via the Lambda Runtime API.

data.title: Lambda Core Concepts
items: **Handler** — the function entry point that Lambda invokes
**Package** — your code and dependencies zipped or containerized
**Trigger** — the event source that invokes your function (API Gateway, S3, SQS, etc.)

data.text: Lambda layers let you package common libraries and dependencies separately from your function code. You can share a single layer across multiple functions. Environment variables store configuration like database URLs and feature flags outside your code.

Every Lambda function runs with an IAM execution role that grants permissions to access AWS resources. Concurrency limits how many instances of your function can run simultaneously. You can set reserved concurrency to prevent a function from consuming all available account concurrency.

Publishing a version creates an immutable snapshot of your function. Aliases are pointers to specific versions and can be updated without changing event sources. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a number of execution environments to eliminate cold starts.

data.title: Python Lambda Function
data.content: A simple Lambda function in Python that processes an S3 event.
data.code:
import json
import boto3

s3_client = boto3.client('s3')

def lambda_handler(event, context):
    for record in event['Records']:
        bucket_name = record['s3']['bucket']['name']
        object_key = record['s3']['object']['key']
        
        response = s3_client.head_object(
            Bucket=bucket_name,
            Key=object_key
        )
        size = response['ContentLength']
        
        print(f"File {object_key} in bucket {bucket_name} is {size} bytes")
        
        return {
            'statusCode': 200,
            'body': json.dumps(f"Processed {object_key}")
        }

data.title: Lambda Best Practices
data.text: Keep functions small and focused on a single task. Use environment variables for configuration. Set appropriate timeouts and memory allocations based on your function's needs.

terms.definition: The initial latency when Lambda creates a new execution environment for a function invocation.
Pre-initialized execution environments that eliminate cold starts for functions with steady traffic.

data.title: Deploy a Lambda Function
data.description: Create a Python Lambda function that returns the current time when invoked.
steps: Create a new Lambda function in the AWS console
Write a handler function that returns the current UTC timestamp
Test the function using the console test tool
Add an environment variable for the timezone
data.expectedOutcome: Your Lambda function returns the current time in JSON format. You can invoke it from the console and see the result.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Lambda runs code without provisioning or managing servers
You pay only for the compute time your code consumes
Layers and environment variables help organize and configure functions
Versions and aliases enable safe deployments and rollbacks
data.takeaway: Lambda is the backbone of serverless on AWS. It integrates with almost every AWS service and lets you build applications without thinking about servers.
